label: New Zealand

parties.name: Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

governmentText.majority: {party} governs alone with {seats} seats, a rare outright majority under MMP.
governmentText.confidence_supply: {lead} governs with confidence and supply from {partner}.
governmentText.minority: {party} leads a minority government on {seats} seats and has to win every vote in the House.
governmentText.hung: No combination reaches a majority. {largest} is the largest party, and the talks begin.

goalHint: Reach {majority} of {total} seats, alone or with partners. Seats follow the party vote, so every region counts, and the Māori electorates are their own battleground.

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Food prices, rents and petrol: the squeeze on every household budget.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Unaffordable homes, KiwiBuild and the rental crunch.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Waiting lists, nurse shortages and a stretched hospital system.

issues.name: Economy & tax
issues.blurb: Tax cuts, capital gains and who pays for the recovery.

issues.name: Climate & environment
issues.blurb: Emissions, farm pollution and clean rivers.

issues.name: Law & order
issues.blurb: Ram raids, gangs and youth crime.

issues.name: COVID-19 response
issues.blurb: Lockdowns, the border and the team of five million.

issues.name: Child poverty
issues.blurb: Kids in cold, damp homes and the promise to halve child poverty.

issues.name: Te Tiriti & co-governance
issues.blurb: Co-governance, Māori rights and the Treaty's place in law.

2008.label: 2008 · Key v. Clark
2008.tagline: November 2008. Helen Clark is after a fourth term, and says the campaign is about trust. John Key is promising change and a tax cut as the economy slips into recession and the world's banks wobble. Winston Peters is fighting for his seat and his party's life. Win a fourth term, or end nine years of Labour.

events.headline: The government's pre-election update on 6 October shows $3.1 billion less tax next year and more borrowing, and {party} has to defend its books just as it asks for a fourth term
National unveils its tax plan on 9 October: around $47 a week more for people on the average wage or above, and {party} claims the economy and the high ground
The Serious Fraud Office clears New Zealand First on 11 October, and {party}'s leader says the whole investigation was a waste of time
At Labour's campaign launch on 12 October Helen Clark guarantees every retail bank deposit, a plan worth $150 billion, and National agrees to back it. {party} is seen to act on the crisis
The Greens say on 20 October they could only form a government with Labour, and {party} clarifies where its votes will go
The Electoral Commission clears New Zealand First on 24 October over donations it failed to declare, but {party} still has to climb back from the damage of the summer
United Future leader Peter Dunne says in late October his party will side with National after six years of backing Labour, and {party} loses a loyal partner
Parliament censures Winston Peters 62 to 56 over the Owen Glenn donation, and {party} cannot shake the whiff of scandal
Labour says John Key did not disclose nearly half his Tranz Rail shares while he was transport spokesman, and {party} has to deal with a question of trust
Petrol has crossed two dollars a litre and inflation is at an eighteen-year high, and voters who feel the squeeze look at {party}
Critics say the Electoral Finance Act has a chilling effect on political activity, and {party} makes it a question of free speech
Polls commissioned by the Marae programme suggest the Māori Party will win most of the Māori electorates, and {party} says it can work with either big party

issues.name: Tax cuts
issues.blurb: National's promise of about $47 a week more for the average earner, and Labour's warning against borrowing for tax cuts.

issues.name: Recession & the banks
issues.blurb: Treasury's August call that the economy was in recession, and Labour's guarantee of every retail bank deposit.

issues.name: Trust
issues.blurb: Helen Clark's theme for the campaign, John Key's Tranz Rail shares and the inquiries into New Zealand First's donations.

issues.name: Food & petrol
issues.blurb: Petrol above two dollars a litre and the highest inflation in eighteen years.

issues.name: Electoral Finance Act
issues.blurb: The new law on election spending and the complaint that it had a chilling effect on political activity.

2011.label: 2011 · Key v. Goff
2011.tagline: November 2011. Christchurch is still burying and rebuilding after the earthquakes, the Rugby World Cup has just been won at home, and John Key is the most popular prime minister in years. National wants to sell stakes in state power companies and Labour's Phil Goff wants to stop it. The voting system itself is on the ballot too. Win a second term, or make Key work for it.

events.headline: The All Blacks win the Rugby World Cup final at Eden Park on 23 October, and the country's good mood rubs off on the government of {party}
Key and Goff meet in the first TVNZ debate on 31 October, and a text poll gives the night to Key with 61%, which steadies {party}'s lead
Key and ACT's John Banks meet over tea in a Newmarket cafe on 11 November to signal an Epsom deal, and a recording of the chat, left running on the table, makes it a scandal for {party}
Winston Peters wins the minor parties' debate on 16 November in the viewers' text poll, with 36%, and {party} is suddenly a story again
Goff wins the TV3 debate on 21 November in front of an audience of undecided voters, and {party} gets its best night of the campaign
National's plan to sell minority stakes in state energy companies keeps polling badly, and voters who dislike it look at {party}
Oil from the grounded container ship Rena keeps washing onto Bay of Plenty beaches, and {party} makes the case against deep sea drilling
Hone Harawira's new Mana party takes aim at the Māori Party in the Māori electorates, and {party} has a fight on its hands
Don Brash takes over as ACT leader to rescue a party polling below the 5% line, but its best hope is still the Epsom seat, and {party} has to rely on National's goodwill

The age of superannuation eligibility comes up in the minor parties' debates on 30 October and 16 November, and Winston Peters says nobody else will defend the pension at 65, which wins {party} a hearing

issues.name: Asset sales
issues.blurb: National's plan to sell minority stakes in state energy companies, and the pledge from Labour and the Greens to stop it.

issues.name: Economy & recovery
issues.blurb: The Christchurch earthquakes, the Rena oil spill and a slow recovery from the recession.

issues.name: Superannuation age
issues.blurb: The age at which people can claim New Zealand Superannuation, and the argument over raising it above 65.

issues.name: Jobs & prices
issues.blurb: Youth unemployment and the cost of food and power for families on ordinary incomes.

issues.name: Environment & mining
issues.blurb: The Emissions Trading Scheme, mining on conservation land and the Rena spill.

issues.name: Voting system referendum
issues.blurb: The referendum held with the election on whether to keep mixed-member proportional voting.

2014.label: 2014 · Key v. Cunliffe
2014.tagline: September 2014. John Key is after a third term with a growing economy and a steady hand. Nicky Hager's book has put National's methods on trial, Labour's David Cunliffe wants a capital gains tax and free doctor visits, and Winston Peters and Kim Dotcom are both in the race. Win the third term, or find a left that adds up.

events.headline: Nicky Hager's Dirty Politics lands on 13 August, drawn from the leaked emails of the blogger Cameron Slater, and {party} answers for its methods for the rest of the campaign
Labour opens its campaign on 10 August with free doctor visits and prescriptions for pregnant women, children under 13 and people over 65, and {party} has something to sell
National launches in South Auckland on 24 August and lets KiwiSaver members spend their tax credits on a first home, and {party} goes after Labour's housing ground
Judith Collins resigns from Cabinet on 30 August after an email suggests she undermined the head of the Serious Fraud Office, and {party} loses a senior minister in the middle of the campaign
In the Christchurch debate on 2 September Key lands a hit when Cunliffe cannot say whether family homes held in trusts would escape Labour's capital gains tax, and {party} loses the economic argument
ACT launches on 7 September with a promise to repeal the Resource Management Act and scrap the Overseas Investment Office, and {party} gives its base something to cheer
Hone Harawira sends party members an expletive-filled email on 8 September about the Internet Party's cannabis push, and {party} looks like a marriage of convenience
Kim Dotcom's Moment of Truth event on 15 September brings Glenn Greenwald, Edward Snowden and Julian Assange into one night on surveillance, and the headlines do not turn into votes for {party}
Key tells supporters on 17 September that if they want a National government they should party vote National, not buy 'a lamb chop' when they want steak, and {party} squeezes its partners

Key and Winston Peters both back Labour's Kelvin Davis in Te Tai Tokerau on 18 September, and Hone Harawira says they are trying to overturn the voters' choice, which costs {party} its electorate lifeline
Winston Peters fills provincial halls on the campaign trail, and {party} climbs
Colin Craig's Conservatives plaster the country with billboards and polls close to the 5% line, and {party} peels votes from the right
Tariana Turia, co-founder of the Māori Party, is standing down at this election, and {party} has to hold its seats without her
The Greens' Russel Norman and Metiria Turei hold steady near 10% and say they want to be in a Labour-led government, and {party} stays in the frame

issues.name: Capital gains tax
issues.blurb: Labour's tax on gains from investment property, National's promise of a surplus, and the row over homes held in family trusts.

issues.name: Dirty Politics
issues.blurb: Nicky Hager's book on the leaked Cameron Slater emails and Judith Collins' resignation as a minister.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Auckland prices out of reach, and National's plan to let KiwiSaver members spend their tax credits on a first home.

issues.name: Free doctor visits
issues.blurb: Labour's promise of free doctor visits and prescriptions for pregnant women, children under 13 and people over 65.

issues.name: Child poverty
issues.blurb: Children in cold, damp homes and the argument over how much help for poor families the government should pay for.

issues.name: Surveillance
issues.blurb: Kim Dotcom's fight with the government and the Moment of Truth event on mass surveillance and the Five Eyes network.

2017.label: 2017 · Ardern v. English
2017.tagline: September 2017. Seven weeks out, Labour swaps Andrew Little for Jacinda Ardern and the race resets overnight. National has nine years in government and a steady hand at the top. Winston Peters waits to be asked.

events.headline: Andrew Little steps aside and Jacinda Ardern takes over seven weeks out. 'Let's do this': {party} surges
Metiria Turei resigns after her benefit fraud admission, and {party} slides toward the 5% line
Details of Winston Peters' pension overpayment leak to the press, and {party} cries dirty politics
Steven Joyce claims an $11.7 billion hole in Labour's costings. Economists say there isn't one, but {party} spends a week defending its numbers
National hammers Labour's tax working group and the spectre of a capital gains tax, and {party} wins back nervous homeowners
Hundreds of farmers protest Labour's water tax in Ardern's home town of Morrinsville, and the provinces lean toward {party}
Bill English's steady-hand pitch on a growing economy reassures the middle, and {party} holds firm
Labour says any tax working group changes will wait until after the 2020 election, closing off National's best line of attack on {party}
James Shaw steadies the Greens with a clean rivers push, and {party} climbs back over 5%
Gareth Morgan's Opportunities Party grabs headlines with a bold tax plan, and {party} peels off restless voters

issues.name: Housing crisis
issues.blurb: Auckland prices, families living in cars and motels, and Labour's KiwiBuild plan for 100,000 homes.

issues.name: Tax
issues.blurb: National's families package of tax cuts, against Labour's tax working group and fears of a capital gains tax.

issues.name: Child poverty
issues.blurb: Children in cold, damp homes, and Ardern's pledge to make cutting child poverty her mission.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Underfunded hospitals, mental health waits and the cost of seeing a GP.

issues.name: Clean rivers & water
issues.blurb: Swimmable rivers, dairy pollution and Labour's proposed royalty on water used for irrigation.

issues.name: Immigration
issues.blurb: Record net migration of about 72,000 a year, and Labour and NZ First promises to cut it.

2020.label: 2020 · Ardern v. Collins
2020.tagline: October 2020. A second Auckland outbreak has pushed the election back a month, Ardern's COVID response is the whole campaign, and National is on its third leader of the year. Win the first single-party majority under MMP, or stop it.

events.headline: COVID returns to Auckland, the city locks down and the election moves to 17 October. The country rallies behind {party}
The Green School grant blows up in James Shaw's face. He calls approving it an error of judgement, and {party} spends the week on the back foot
A $4 billion error turns up in National's fiscal plan, and {party} loses the economy argument it needed
Collins comes out fighting in the first TVNZ debate and claims victory, which steadies {party}
The Serious Fraud Office charges two people over the NZ First Foundation's donations, and {party} cannot get off the ropes
Gun owners, farmers and refugees from National's chaos lift {party} to its best polling in years
Caucus leaks keep coming under National's third leader of the year, and {party} cannot stay on message
Selfie queues at every stop: the campaign trail looks like a victory lap for {party}
The cannabis referendum energises young voters, and {party} signs them up
Rawiri Waititi's Waiariki campaign gathers pace, and {party} smells a comeback

issues.name: COVID-19 response
issues.blurb: The second Auckland lockdown, managed isolation at the border and the elimination strategy.

issues.name: Economy & recovery
issues.blurb: The deepest recession in decades, wage subsidies, and a new 39% tax rate on income over $180,000.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Record house prices despite the pandemic, and KiwiBuild's missed targets.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Cancer drug funding, mental health services and hospital waiting lists.

issues.name: Cannabis & euthanasia votes
issues.blurb: Two referendums on the same ballot: legal recreational cannabis and the End of Life Choice Act.

issues.name: Climate & environment
issues.blurb: The Zero Carbon Act's targets, new freshwater rules for farmers, and the Green School grant row.

2023.label: 2023 · Luxon v. Hipkins
2023.tagline: October 2023. Ardern is gone, Hipkins has burned half the policy programme, and the cost of living is eating everything else. National leads but needs ACT, and maybe Winston Peters. Hold the left together, or build a three-party right.

events.headline: Hipkins burns half of Labour's programme and promises 'bread and butter'. Some voters give {party} a second look
Justice Minister Kiri Allan resigns after a car crash and an arrest, the latest minister to fall, and {party} looks tired
Senior MP Michael Woodhouse says he will stand only in his electorate after a row over his list ranking, and {party} spends the day on an internal dispute
Labour promises to take GST off fruit and vegetables. Shoppers like it, economists do not, and {party} gets a modest lift
Economists pick apart the foreign buyer tax that pays for National's tax cuts, and {party} spends a week on the defensive
Luxon says he would pick up the phone to Winston Peters if he had to, and {party} surges past 5%
A young Te Pāti Māori candidate, Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke, takes on Nanaia Mahuta in Hauraki-Waikato, and the Māori electorates swing toward {party}
Another week of ram raids puts law and order on the front page, and {party} owns the issue
ACT promises a referendum on the Treaty principles, firing up its base and handing {party} the headlines
Hipkins rules out a wealth tax and a capital gains tax if Labour is re-elected, and left voters drift to {party}
After the Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, climate stays on the agenda and {party} gains

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Food inflation that peaked above 12%, mortgage rates near 7%, and Labour's plan to take GST off fruit and vegetables.

issues.name: Tax cuts
issues.blurb: National's income tax relief, paid for partly by a foreign buyer tax, and Labour ruling out a wealth tax.

issues.name: Law & order
issues.blurb: Ram raids, gang patches and National's military-style academies for serious young offenders.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Nurse and doctor shortages, emergency department waits, and the DHBs merged into Te Whatu Ora.

issues.name: Co-governance
issues.blurb: Three Waters, the Māori Health Authority and ACT's call for a referendum on the Treaty principles.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Prices off their peak but rents rising, and National's plan to restore interest deductions for landlords.

issues.name: Climate & the floods
issues.blurb: Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods, and plans to price farm emissions.

events.headline: Grim GDP figures lead the six o'clock news, putting pressure on {party}
Another record rent rise puts housing on the front page, and voters look to {party}
{party}'s leader wins the televised leaders' debate, and the worm agrees
A candidate's old social media posts resurface, and {party} spends the day apologising
MMP maths has voters thinking about coalitions, and tactical support drifts to {party}
{party}'s leader fumbles a costings question on morning radio
Business groups and the papers line up behind {party}
A viral moment breaks for {party} among first-time voters
A bus tour through the provinces wins {party} friendly local coverage
A natural disaster puts leadership first, and {party} looks the part
TVNZ offers {party} a head-to-head debate slot
events.prompt: A prime-time debate is on the table. How do you play it?

choices.text: Accept and go on the attack
choices.resultText: You land blows and take a few. The overnight polls twitch your way.
A steady, on-message night. No gaffes, no fireworks.
You dodge the studio lights. The press calls it a snub.

events.headline: Every interview asks {party} the same question: who would you govern with?
events.prompt: Voters want to know your coalition partners. What do you say?

choices.text: Name your partners and campaign as a bloc
choices.resultText: Clarity reassures your side. The other side calls it a stitch-up.
Nobody is ruled out, and nobody is quite reassured.

choices.text: Rule out the kingmaker and dare voters to choose
choices.resultText: A bold line. It sharpens the contrast with your rival.

events.headline: {party}'s caucus is split on the big tax pledge
events.prompt: The manifesto goes to print on Friday. Which way do you push?

choices.text: Go bold with a defining, risky pledge
choices.resultText: The base roars. Treasury officials start sharpening pencils.

choices.text: Play it safe: no hostages to fortune
Make it a contrast with the rival's costings
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.
